Chap 5 You own a house with one acre of land on Main Street in your hometown. The property has been in your family for three generations. You have so many vivid memories of good times with your grandparents, parents, spouse, and two children there. Just last week, a local government official knocked on your front door. The official informed you that the town was taking the front one-half acre of your property (your house sits on the back one-half acre) for the purpose of widening Main Street and that the government would be issuing you a check for $15,000 for the one-half acre. You are taken aback. Just last year, you had your property (just the land, not the house) appraised, and the one acre you own was appraised at $60,000. By simple logic and math, you interpret the appraisal to mean that one-half acre of the property is worth $30,000, not $15,000 as the government has offered. Further, the fact that the government is taking the front one-half acre of your land means that once Main Street is widened, your house will sit closer to the road, thereby depriving you and your family of the peace and tranquility of the one-half acre setback and buffer. All things considered, you do not want to give up the one-half acre—again, the property has been in your family for three generations, and given the fact that you have two children, you would like to ultimately extend that to four generations. Which of the following is true in this scenario?
choices: You are protected by the Takings Clause of the U.S. Constitution but not the Due Process Clause.

You are entitled to base compensation of $30,000 (one-half of the appraisal value) for your one-half acre of property, plus an additional amount to account for your emotional attachment to the property not to exceed three times the base compensation amount.
You are entitled to reject the government’s offer, which would effectively terminate the government’s attempted taking of your one-half acre of property.
You are entitled to a fair price for your one-half acre of property.

Additionally, you would like to have a doctor of your choosing examine her arm and assess the true extent of the injuries. Chap 8 Your best friend Abigail is undergoing a contentious divorce that has necessitated a court proceeding. Abigail has called you as her “star” witness to testify against Raj, her soon-to-be ex-spouse. Prior to the proceeding, Abigail implored you to “be creative” in your testimony so that she will receive a favorable ruling; after all, she says, “That’s what best friends are for.” In response to Abigail’s cajoling, you take the witness stand and testify that Raj has had at least three extramarital affairs in the five years he has been married to Abigail and that he has frequently abused her, both physically and psychologically. None of this is factual, and you know it. Which of the following is true regarding your testimony?
choices: You have slandered Raj, but you have not committed perjury because your testimony was at Abigail’s instigation and insistence.
You have committed perjury, and you have slandered Raj.
Your testimony is subject to a limited privilege.
